headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk from shared-bus Pipecat feeding Unstructured’s file-processing pipeline; capability conflict is also present.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a uses a shared bus/session scope and can emit text, while agent_b reads files and processes documents by default. That creates a plausible path where attacker-controlled content from A is ingested by B as trusted instructions. The interaction is documented only at profile level, so uncertainty remains, but the shared bus makes this more than manual copy-paste.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs are forwarded onto the shared bus into agent_b’s document inputs, injection is possible.
IF agent_b treats file or text content as instructions without provenance checks, attacker-controlled content can steer behavior.
mitigations: Separate the bus from document inputs with a typed schema.
Add provenance tags to all agent_a outputs before B consumes them.
Disable automatic instruction-following on untrusted text in B.
Review one sample A→B message path for prompt-like content.
requires-engineering: add content sanitization and allowlist parsing at the handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches conversation state, audio/video/images/text and has allowlisted network egress; agent_b reads and writes files and also has allowlisted egress. If A’s outputs or transcripts are placed into B’s workspace, B can persist or transmit sensitive content. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this is inferred rather than directly observed.
conditions: IF agent_a conversation state or transcripts are written into agent_b’s workspace, leakage risk exists.
IF agent_b uploads processed documents or extracted text to its backend, sensitive content can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate workspaces.
Block B from reading A’s runtime state files.
Turn off any automatic upload path for B during tests.
Inspect one end-to-end run for unexpected file copies.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation and egress policy.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b can read/write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; agent_a supports multiple instances on a shared bus and can also use stdin/stdout. That overlap can create race conditions or clobbering if both touch the same artifacts. The profiles do not show locking or a shared directory, so the conflict is plausible but not proven.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or file names, collisions can occur.
IF the orchestrator does not provide locks, concurrent runs can overwrite each other’s outputs.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Use unique per-run filenames.
Run only one writer at a time for shared artifacts.
Check for lock support in the orchestrator.
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transactional writes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate conversational text and extracted content, and agent_b is a document-processing pipeline that may consume that text downstream. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into parsed documents or derived outputs. No verification step is documented in either profile, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests agent_a output without validation, A’s mistakes propagate.
IF downstream actions rely on B’s parsed result, a single upstream error can affect multiple work products.
mitigations: Insert a human review step for A→B handoffs.
Compare B output against source documents on one sample.
Mark A output as untrusted metadata.
Reject outputs lacking source citations.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks between A and B.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are docs-only open-source components with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch documented. agent_a handles richer media and analytics, while agent_b processes documents and images, but the profiles do not show a concrete compliance conflict. Because the evidence is sparse, I do not escalate beyond low.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is routed through a noncompliant deployment of either agent, compliance risk increases.
IF retention or logging settings differ between the two deployments, policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Confirm both deployments’ retention settings.
Avoid routing regulated data through either agent until policies are checked.
Document the data classes each agent may see.
Review privacy policy links for B and docs for A.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across the pair.
